The six-week corporate retreat timeline

By James Carter, founder of Legendary Team Building · Updated August 2026
Corporate retreats4 min readBy James Carter, founder of Legendary Team Building
Quick answer

Most retreats don’t fail on the day — they fail six weeks earlier, when the venue wasn’t locked and the outcome wasn’t clear. This corporate retreat timeline is a simple six-week countdown: what to lock and when, so nothing important gets left to the last week.

Six weeks is comfortable for most single-location retreats (give larger groups or peak-season venues more). The rule underneath the whole timeline: secure the long poles — outcome, venue, travel — first, and let the agenda follow. Here’s the countdown.

  • 6 weeks out — Lock the outcome

    Get sponsor sign-off on the one thing the retreat must produce, confirm the dates, and settle who actually needs to be in the room. Everything downstream serves this. Start with the sponsor questions.

  • 5 weeks out — Book venue & travel

    The long poles. Secure the room and the flights before you touch the agenda — availability drives everything else. Use the venue checklist.

  • 4 weeks out — Draft the agenda

    Build it backwards from the outcome as a breath pattern, and choose the experience or activity that anchors the day. See the agenda shapes and activities.

  • 3 weeks out — Confirm logistics

    Catering, A/V and materials. Send the invite with logistics and any pre-work so people arrive ready.

  • 2 weeks out — Finalize the run-of-show

    Brief facilitators, confirm headcount and dietary needs, and lock the minute-by-minute.

  • 1 week out — Reconfirm everything

    Re-touch every vendor, print materials, and send attendees the final details and directions.

  • Day of & after — Run and follow up

    Run the day, capture commitments in the room, and send the commitments and photos within 48 hours while it’s still warm — then work the 30 days after, below.

The 30 days after — where retreats stick or die

Most offsites die on the flight home. The countdown gets you to a good day; these three moves are what make it still true a month later. None of them takes more than fifteen minutes.

  • Within 48 hours — Send it back

    Send the commitments exactly as people said them — names, owners, dates — plus the photos. Do it while the room is still warm; a week later it reads as homework.

  • Week 2 — One prompt each

    A single question to every person: what’s one thing you’ve done differently since? Short, individual, and it keeps the retreat present without another meeting.

  • Day 30 — The check-in

    A 30-minute check-in: what held, what slipped, what we’re changing. Put it on the calendar before anyone leaves the room — Day 30 lands far better when it isn’t a surprise. A simple way to make it real: before people scatter, each person names one small, daily behaviour entirely in their own control and tracks it privately for thirty days.

Frequently asked questions

How far in advance should you plan a corporate retreat? +

Six to eight weeks is comfortable for most single-location retreats; larger groups or peak-season venues want about three months. Lock the venue and travel first.

What is the first step in planning a company retreat? +

Lock the outcome. Get sponsor sign-off on the one thing the retreat must produce before you book anything — the whole plan serves it. The sponsor questions get you there.

When should you book the retreat venue? +

Early — around five weeks out for a single-location retreat, earlier for large groups or peak season. Venue and travel are the long poles that constrain everything else.

What should you do after the retreat? +

Send the follow-up within 48 hours while it’s warm — the captured commitments, owners and dates. The days after are where a retreat either sticks or evaporates.
